chapters.title: Chapter 3: Duration: Measuring Interest Rate Risk

lessons.title: PV01 and Rupee Duration: Measuring Risk in Rupees per Basis Point

children.text: Modified duration tells you a bond moves about 4% for every 1% change in yield. Useful, but no one on a bond desk thinks in whole percentage points. RBI usually moves rates in steps of 25 basis points or more, and G-Sec yields routinely shift 3 to 8 basis points in a day. And percentages hide scale: a modified duration of 7 on ₹5 lakh and on ₹5 crore are very different risks. So traders, treasury heads and portfolio managers compress everything into one rupee number: how much do I make or lose for every single basis point? That number is PV01, and this lesson shows you how to calculate it, add it up across a portfolio and use it to control risk.

body.text: PV01 is the rupee change in a position's value for a 1 basis point change in yield. Unlike duration, PV01s can simply be added across bonds, so it tells you in one number how much a whole portfolio is betting on interest rates.

children.text: Two Rupee Measures of Rate Risk

markDefs.definition: Modified duration multiplied by the market value of a position. The approximate rupee change in value for a 100% (1.00) change in yield. Also called money duration or dollar duration.
Present value of a basis point: the approximate rupee change in a position's value for a 1 basis point (0.01%) change in yield. Also called PVBP or DV01.

children.text: Start with
rupee duration

: modified duration multiplied by the market value of what you hold. On its own it is an awkward number, since it describes a 100 percentage point move that never happens. Divide it by 10,000 and you get something every bond trader in India uses daily:
PV01
, the rupees gained or lost per basis point.

body.caption: Market value should be the full (dirty) value of the position: price including accrued interest, times the units held.
Estimated rupee change for any move: PV01 × number of basis points.

children.text: Worked Example: Priya's ₹10 Lakh Position
Priya Sethi from the last lesson holds ₹10 lakh market value of the illustrative 7.10% G-Sec with five years left, at a 6.80% yield. Its modified duration is 4.1589.

Check it against full repricing. If the yield rises exactly 1 basis point to 6.81%, Priya's position falls by ₹415.78; if it falls 1 basis point to 6.79%, it rises by ₹415.99. The PV01 of ₹415.89 sits right between the two. For a single basis point, convexity is negligible, which is why PV01 is so reliable for day-to-day risk.

body.text: PV01 is the language of Indian bond markets. Bank treasuries report their investment book's PV01 to risk committees, mutual fund risk teams track portfolio PV01, and traders on the NDS-OM and RFQ platforms size positions by it. When a trader says a position is "₹5 lakh a bip", they mean its PV01 is ₹5 lakh: every basis point move in yields makes or loses ₹5 lakh.

body.title: Calculate a PV01
body.prompt: You hold ₹25 lakh market value of an illustrative SDL with a modified duration of 6.8. What is the PV01 of your position, in rupees?
body.explanation: PV01 = 6.8 × ₹25,00,000 × 0.0001 = ₹1,700. A 10 basis point rise in yields would cost about ₹17,000, and a 50 basis point rise about ₹85,000.

children.text: The Real Power: PV01s Add Up

Duration is a ratio, so you cannot add the durations of two bonds together; you have to weight them by market value first. PV01 is already in rupees, so you just add. Here is an illustrative ₹45 lakh bond portfolio held by Suresh and Anita Menon, a doctor couple in Kochi.

body.caption: The Menons' bond portfolio: money invested vs rate risk carried

body.title: Share of Money vs Share of Rate Risk (%)

children.text: The 30-year G-Sec holds just 22% of the Menons' money but nearly 40% of their interest rate risk. The 5-year G-Sec, their largest holding, carries barely a quarter. The portfolio's total PV01 of ₹3,130 means a 50 basis point rise in yields would cost about ₹1,56,500. And the portfolio's modified duration, 6.95, is just the total PV01 converted back: ₹3,130 × 10,000 ÷ ₹45,00,000.

body.title: Where the Menons' ₹3,130 PV01 Comes From
Adding up risk
body.question: You hold two bonds: ₹10 lakh with a modified duration of 3 and ₹30 lakh with a modified duration of 9. Which statement is correct?
options: The portfolio's modified duration is 12, the sum of the two durations
The portfolio's modified duration is 6, the simple average of the two
The portfolio's PV01 is ₹3,000 (₹300 + ₹2,700), and its modified duration is 7.5
PV01 cannot be combined across bonds with different maturities
body.explanation: PV01s add directly: ₹10,00,000 × 3 × 0.0001 = ₹300, plus ₹30,00,000 × 9 × 0.0001 = ₹2,700, for ₹3,000. Converting back: ₹3,000 × 10,000 ÷ ₹40,00,000 = 7.5. Durations cannot be summed, and a simple average ignores that most of the money sits in the longer bond.

columns.label: Modified duration
points: A percentage: sensitivity per 1% yield change
Same for ₹1 lakh or ₹100 crore of the same bond
Compares the riskiness of bonds or funds
Must be value-weighted to combine across holdings

columns.label: PV01
points: A rupee amount: gain or loss per 1 basis point
Grows with the size of the position
Measures how much money is actually at risk
Adds directly across holdings to give total portfolio risk

children.text: Using PV01 to Swap and Hedge

Because PV01 puts every bond on the same rupee scale, it answers "how much of bond B equals the rate risk of bond A?" Divide the two PV01s per rupee, which is the same as dividing their modified durations. For example, how much of the 30-year G-Sec carries the same rate risk as the Menons' ₹20 lakh in the 5-year G-Sec?

body.caption: About ₹6.67 lakh of the 30-year bond has the same PV01 as ₹20 lakh of the 5-year bond.

children.text: Institutions use exactly this ratio to hedge. A bank holding long G-Secs that wants to cut its rate risk without selling can take an offsetting position with the same PV01, for example by selling interest rate futures on the NSE or entering an overnight indexed swap. Individuals rarely hedge this way, but the same logic tells you how much rate risk you remove when you sell one bond and buy another.

body.title: Match PV01 across bonds
body.prompt: The Menons want to offset the rate risk of their ₹10 lakh in the 30-year G-Sec (modified duration 12.47) using the 10-year SDL (modified duration 7.00). How much SDL, in lakh rupees, has the same PV01? Round to two decimal places.
body.explanation: Equivalent amount = ₹10 lakh × 12.4724 ÷ 7.0038 = ₹17.81 lakh. Both positions have a PV01 of about ₹1,247. Because the SDL is less rate-sensitive, it takes nearly ₹1.8 of SDL to match every ₹1 of the 30-year bond.

body.title: Decode the jargon
body.textWithBlank: PV01 stands for the present value of one ___.
body.explanation: One basis point is 0.01%, or 0.0001 as a decimal. PV01, also written PVBP or DV01, is the rupee value change for a one basis point move in yield.

body.title: Fine print: when PV01 needs care

children.text: Use market value, not face value.
₹10 lakh face value of a bond at ₹92 has a market value of ₹9.2 lakh plus accrued interest, and its PV01 is based on that.
PV01 changes over time.
As a bond ages its duration shortens, and as yields move its price and duration change, so recalculate regularly.
Multiplying PV01 by large moves inherits duration's error.
PV01 × 200 overstates the loss from a 200 basis point rise, because it ignores convexity.
A portfolio PV01 assumes every yield moves together.
If 5-year yields rise 10 bps and 30-year yields fall 5 bps, the Menons' total PV01 cannot tell you the outcome. Professionals track PV01 bucket by bucket along the yield curve for this reason.

body.title: Deepak sets a risk limit
body.scenario: Deepak Arora runs the investments of his family's business in Kolkata. Its ₹1.2 crore bond portfolio holds ₹50 lakh of the 5-year 7.10% G-Sec (modified duration 4.16), ₹40 lakh of the 10-year 7.30% SDL (modified duration 7.00) and ₹30 lakh of the 30-year 7.00% G-Sec (modified duration 12.47), all at the yields in the Menons' example. The family's rule: a sudden 50 basis point rise in yields must not cost more than ₹3 lakh.
body.prompt: Calculate the portfolio's PV01 and its loss from a 50 bp rise. Is it within the limit? If not, can Deepak fix it by switching the 30-year G-Sec into the 5-year G-Sec? Suggest a switch that would work, assuming 364-day T-bills have a modified duration of about 0.95.
body.modelAnswer:
1. PV01 by holding: 5-year = ₹50,00,000 × 4.1589 × 0.0001 = ₹2,079; SDL = ₹40,00,000 × 7.0038 × 0.0001 = ₹2,802; 30-year = ₹30,00,000 × 12.4724 × 0.0001 = ₹3,742. Total PV01 ≈ ₹8,623.
2. A 50 bp rise costs about ₹8,623 × 50 = ₹4,31,000, well above the ₹3 lakh limit. The portfolio's modified duration is ₹8,623 × 10,000 ÷ ₹1.2 crore ≈ 7.19.
3. The limit implies a maximum PV01 of ₹3,00,000 ÷ 50 = ₹6,000, so Deepak must remove about ₹2,623 of PV01.
4. Switching into the 5-year G-Sec: each ₹1 lakh moved cuts PV01 by ₹1,00,000 × (12.4724 − 4.1589) × 0.0001 ≈ ₹83. Removing ₹2,623 would need about ₹31.5 lakh moved, more than the ₹30 lakh he holds. Even selling all of the 30-year bond into the 5-year leaves PV01 at about ₹6,129, still over the limit.
5. Switching into 364-day T-bills: each ₹1 lakh moved cuts PV01 by ₹1,00,000 × (12.4724 − 0.95) × 0.0001 ≈ ₹115. Removing ₹2,623 needs about ₹22.8 lakh moved from the 30-year G-Sec into T-bills, leaving about ₹7.2 lakh in the 30-year bond. That meets the limit.
6. Deepak should also recheck PV01 every few months, since durations drift, and remember that PV01 × 50 slightly overstates the actual loss because of convexity, which gives a small extra cushion.

cards.definition: One hundredth of a percentage point: 0.01%, or 0.0001 as a decimal.
Modified duration × market value. Also called money duration.
Rupee duration ÷ 10,000. The rupee value change for a 1 basis point move in yield. Also PVBP or DV01.
The simple sum of each holding's PV01.
Amount of A × modified duration of A ÷ modified duration of B.

points: Rupee duration = modified duration × market value. PV01 = rupee duration ÷ 10,000.
PV01 is the rupee gain or loss for a 1 basis point change in yield: ₹415.89 on Priya's ₹10 lakh at a modified duration of 4.16.
For a single basis point, PV01 matches full repricing almost exactly, so it is the standard day-to-day risk measure.
PV01s add directly across holdings. The Menons' 30-year G-Sec is 22% of their money but 40% of their rate risk.
Portfolio modified duration = total PV01 × 10,000 ÷ total market value.
The ratio of modified durations tells you how much of one bond matches the rate risk of another, the basis of swaps and hedges.
Use market value, recalculate regularly, and remember PV01 assumes every yield moves together.

body.text: This lesson is for education only and is not investment advice. Portfolios, bonds, yields, durations and investors are illustrative. PV01 is an approximation that assumes parallel yield moves and ignores convexity for large shifts. Hedging with interest rate futures or swaps involves additional risks and is typically suited to institutions. Consult a SEBI-registered investment adviser before making portfolio decisions.
